subject: Anthropology
title: NGOs and Governance
description: Learn NGOs and Governance in one minute.

hook.text: In parts of Africa, an NGO provides more services than the government. Who really governs when the state withdraws?

buildup.text: NGOs fill gaps left by weak or retreating states, delivering health, education, and development services to millions.

discovery.text: They form a parallel governance system, often funded by foreign donors with their own agendas and priorities.

twist.text: NGOs can undermine state capacity. When aid replaces government, accountability shifts from citizens to donors.

climax.text: NGOs reveal new governance beyond the state. Power increasingly flows through organizations, not just governments.

punchline.text: Governance now extends far beyond the state.

quiz.question: How can NGOs undermine state capacity?
options: By replacing government services and shifting accountability to donors

details.summary: Non-governmental organizations increasingly perform governance functions — delivering healthcare, education, and infrastructure — that states fail to provide. This raises questions about accountability, sovereignty, and whether NGOs substitute for or undermine state responsibility.
details.whyItMatters: NGOs now shape policy and deliver services in ways that significantly affect people's lives. Understanding their political role reveals how governance operates beyond formal state institutions and who actually controls development.
takeaways: NGOs increasingly perform governance functions traditionally held by states
Their role raises questions about accountability and sovereignty
NGO governance operates outside democratic accountability structures

faq.question: How do NGOs become political actors?
faq.answer: By providing services that states should deliver — healthcare, education, water — NGOs gain political influence in communities. They set priorities, define problems, and allocate resources.

faq.question: Are NGOs accountable to the populations they serve?
faq.answer: Often not. NGOs are typically accountable to donors, not beneficiaries. Communities cannot vote out an NGO or demand different services. This creates a democratic deficit where significant governance functions operate outside the accountability structures that democratic theory requires.
